answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
Consequential Accounting is how to measure real world carbon impact in the power sector. Attributional inventories, including LBM and MBM, do not measure impact. Their purpose is to accurately account for usage of clean electricity (MWhs, not MTCO2e). While this is an important foundation, we see many benefits to Consequential Accounting as a path to impactful investment in renewable energy projects.

Send the right investment signal to the market to increase market participation and accelerate decarbonization of power generation. Decision-useful data are available to guide procurement choices for the most impactful projects by accounting for the emissions impact of electricity projects. Boston University is located in one of the cleanest grids in the US. When we procured renewable energy to match our load, we were very intentional, focused on finding a project that would displace the greatest greenhouse gas generation possible in the United States. In 2018 we used marginal emissions data from dirtier grids and compared it with generation profiles provided by wind and solar developers to determine which project would have the greatest impact possible in the displacement of carbon intense power generation on the grid. We chose a vPPA in South Dakota because the marginal generation units likely to be displaced by the wind farm were the dirtiest generators. We chose the project that would displace the most greenhouse gas intense power generation of 127 projects from which we had bids.

Doing this sends an investment signal to build new projects where they have the highest emissions impact. Collectively, this accelerates grid decarbonization – this supports the mission of the GHGP. Consequential Accounting does not rely on deliverability boundaries, opening investment to high impact regions.

Consequential Accounting should be integrated with Scope 2 Accounting. If consequential accounting isn’t included as part of the inventory analysis, how can renewable energy investment impact emissions reductions? If not integrated, Consequential Accounting (with both avoided and induced emissions) should be encouraged as a recommended alternative to Scope 2 Accounting.

answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text:
For Consequential Accounting to be useful, it needs to include avoided and induced emissions, along with additionality, of course. An absolute number for avoided emissions is not useful without comparing it to induced emissions. While Scope 2 accounting doesn’t currently include Consequential Accounting, at Boston University, we share our emissions impact beyond MWh accounting. We do this by comparing the avoided emissions from the displaced marginal generators in South Dakota with the emissions induced by our load in Boston.

The emissions impact formula provided as is accounts for the avoided emissions from a renewable energy project but fails to account for any additional emissions impact from placing a renewable energy project in a non-local grid dirtier than the grid where the load is located. The formula should include both the avoided emissions from the renewable energy project and the induced emissions from the local grid to account for the net emissions impact from the project. In our GHG accounting, Boston University accounts for the avoided emissions that match our induced emissions from the electricity we consume.

Additionally, while not considered in our total emissions inventory, we calculate the additional emissions avoided by BU Wind being located in South Dakota rather than Massachusetts to show the emissions impact associated with the wind project. See Boston University’s renewable energy procurement impact is illustrated on the University’s abatement curve here: https://www.bu.edu/sustainability/vision-progress/data-dashboard/ with monthly data here: https://buildingos.com/reports/dashboards/f6819abaf7d411f0872402420a000186

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text: Reporting emissions impacts each year is a more accurate accounting of the project’s actual impact against baseline and can keep us aware of these impacts.

answers.label: Requiredness of the financial analysis test
Requiredness of the common practice test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text: Additionality is an important driver to accelerate renewable energy development. It is critical to credible claims that an organization has caused a new renewable energy resource to be added to the generation capacity of a region. The regulatory and timing tests should be required as they are more accessible tests that can be documented. Additionality tests should not be so stringent that they impede clean energy investment through financial tests that are not feasible or a positive list that excludes impactful projects. The other tests should be optional and be considered to add to the credibility of the procurement of the project.

answers.label: Context on test feasibility
answers.text: The feasibility of certain tests will depend on the grid region and data availability, so not all tests are feasible across all contexts. Therefore, tests beyond the Regulatory and Timing Tests should be optional.

answers.label: Regions warranting different tests, with examples
answers.text: To account for regional differences, multiple additionality tests should be allowed. The level of rigor should also depend on the type of claim an organization wants to make. In the spirit of providing feasible guidance, multiple pathways should be available to organizations that want to fund/build additional clean power.
